sections.html:
A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the grantor lawfully has and promises nothing about it. Sec. 706.10(4) says it passes all of the interest in or appurtenant to the land that the grantor could lawfully convey, without warranting or implying the existence, quantity or quality of that interest.

With no guarantee of clear title, the buyer's title company may or may not accept one, so ask early. A warranty deed works differently. Under sec. 706.10(5) it includes covenants that the grantor is lawfully seized of the land, has the right to convey it, and that it is free of encumbrance.

A conveyance is valid once it identifies the parties, land and interest, is signed by each grantor and is delivered. Read the deed closely before signing.

A Wisconsin conveyance has to satisfy the formal requisites in sec. 706.02, and a deed headed for recording faces a few formatting rules on top. Go down this list before you take the deed to the register of deeds.

  • It names the parties, the land, and the interest conveyed.
  • Each grantor signs it, or someone signs for the grantor.
  • It is delivered to the grantee.
  • If it gives up a married person's interest in a homestead, each spouse signs or joins in by a separate conveyance. Transfers between spouses are the exception.
  • It carries a form of authentication allowed by sec. 706.06 or ch. 140, and filers are told to bring a notarized deed to the register.
  • It describes the land well enough for the county indexes and, for most documents, includes the full legal description.

The register may turn away a document that does not substantially follow the format rules in sec. 59.43(2m). The document's title sits between 0.5 and 6 inches from the top of page one. That page needs a blank 3 inch by 3 inch space in the upper right corner for recording information, plus return information. Paper is white, at least 20 pound, 8.5 inches wide and 11 or 14 inches long. Ink is black, blue or red. Where the county requires one, add the parcel identification number from the tax bill.

A quitclaim skips the transfer fee only if the transfer fits a statutory exemption. For every conveyance that is not exempt, the grantor pays 30 cents per $100 of value, or $3 per $1,000, collected by the register when the deed is submitted for recording.

Value means the full actual consideration, liens included. For a gift, a deed for nominal consideration or an exchange, it means the estimated open market price. So a no-money quitclaim between relatives is still measured by market value unless an exemption applies, and the deed must cite the exemption by subsection number on its face.

Type of transferSec. 77.25 subsection
Corrects or confirms a prior recorded deed, for nominal, inadequate or no consideration(3)
Parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, parent and son-in-law or daughter-in-law, grandparent and grandchild, for nominal or no consideration(8)
Between husband and wife(8m)
Between an individual and a domestic partner under ch. 770(8n)
Between agent and principal, or trustee to beneficiary without actual consideration(9)
By will, descent or survivorship(11)
Real estate worth $1,000 or less(13)

This is a selection, so read the full text of sec. 77.25 for your relationship. A transfer that fits no subsection owes the fee. The register need not check the value or the exemption claimed, but the Department of Revenue does. If it finds the value understated by 25% or more, or an exemption improperly claimed, it assesses the greater of $25 or 25% of the additional fee. Deliberately falsifying value can bring a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in county jail, or both.

Start online: file a real estate transfer return, print the receipt, and bring it with the notarized deed and payment to the register of deeds in the county where the land lies. Some counties take the package electronically, so check the county website.

The return is filed in the Department of Revenue's My Tax Account system with no username or password. Pick the county, then Quit claim deed as the document type. The conveyance date is when the deed is signed and delivered. List every grantor and grantee, with spouses entered as separate people. If the property was not appraised, the estimated value can come from the latest property tax bill. The system shows only the exemption numbers that fit the document and parties you entered.

Recording costs $30 per document, paid in advance. The register stamps the date, hour and minute on each document and records them in the order received. A document containing an individual's Social Security number cannot be recorded, so keep it off the deed.

Name an authorized recipient and supply adequate postage, and the register mails the recorded document to that person. If several related documents arrive as one transaction and one fails the format rules, the whole group can come back unrecorded, so submit a clean deed. For return questions, write RETR@wisconsin.gov or call (608) 264-6885.

Do not sit on the deed. Under sec. 706.08, an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser for value whose conveyance is recorded first.

sections.h2: Using a quitclaim when you sell
sections.html:
It can work if the buyer and title company accept it. Since a quitclaim carries no warranty, find out which deed form they require before signing anything.

The exemptions in sec. 77.25 point to the usual non-sale uses: transfers within a family, between spouses, and deeds that correct a prior recorded deed.

For a house that needs repairs, has back taxes or comes from an estate, a cash sale as-is is another route. Compare what each offer pays at closing and ask who covers the transfer fee, which the statute puts on the grantor.

Before using a quitclaim to remove someone from the title of a mortgaged home, ask the lender and a Wisconsin attorney what your situation calls for. A deed giving up a spouse's homestead interest needs both spouses to sign.

A short order of work helps: confirm the deed form the buyer wants, gather the legal description and parcel number from the tax bill, file the transfer return, get the deed notarized, then record it and keep the recorded copy with your papers.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed enough to transfer a house in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: Yes, if it meets sec. 706.02. It must identify the parties, land and interest, be signed by each grantor and be delivered, and it should be recorded so it holds against later purchasers. It passes the grantor's interest with no warranty.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: Recording runs $30 per document. A transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value applies too, unless sec. 77.25 exempts the transfer, and the grantor pays it. Copies cost $2 for the first page and $1 for each added page.

faqs.q: Do I need a notary for a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: A recorded deed needs a form of authentication allowed by sec. 706.06 or ch. 140, and filers are told to bring a notarized deed to the register of deeds. Ask your county register about any local requirement.

faqs.q: Does a spouse have to sign a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: If the deed gives up a married person's interest in a homestead, each spouse must sign or join by separate conveyance. Conveyances between spouses are the exception under sec. 706.02(1)(f).

faqs.q: Where do I file a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: With the register of deeds of the county where the real estate is located. File the transfer return with the Department of Revenue first, then bring the receipt to the register.
